title: How is Kibana configured in your project, and how does the ELK stack enable centralized logging and request tracing with correlation IDs?
shortTitle: Kibana configuration and how the ELK stack enables centralized logging and request tracing with correlation IDs
topicTitle: How is Kibana configured in your project

s1_definition.profdef: The ELK stack is three tools working together: Elasticsearch stores and indexes logs for fast search, Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect and parse logs from every service and ship them to Elasticsearch, and Kibana is the web interface for searching, visualising, and dashboarding those logs. Centralized logging means every microservice writes structured JSON logs that are shipped into one searchable Elasticsearch cluster instead of sitting in files on scattered Pods. Request tracing with correlation IDs means each incoming request is assigned a unique identifier that is attached to every log line produced while handling it and propagated to downstream services, so in Kibana you can filter by that one ID and see the complete journey of a single request across every service it touched.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has fifty branches, each keeping its own paper logbook. When a customer complains "my transfer failed," staff would have to phone every branch and flip through separate books. ELK is like scanning every branch's logbook into one central searchable computer. The correlation ID is like stamping a single reference number on every form a customer's request touches as it moves from the teller to the back office to the vault — so later you type that one number into Kibana and instantly see every step the request took, in order, no matter which department handled it.
s1_definition.oneliner: ELK pools every service's logs into one searchable place, and a correlation ID lets you pull the complete story of a single request out of billions of log lines with one filter.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The ELK stack is three tools working together: Elasticsearch stores and indexes logs for fast search, Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect and parse logs from every service and ship them to Elasticsearch, and Kibana is the web interface for searching, visualising, and dashboarding those logs. Centralized logging means every microservice writes structured JSON logs that are shipped into one searchable Elasticsearch cluster instead of sitting in files on scattered Pods. Request tracing with correlation IDs means each incoming request is assigned a unique identifier that is attached to every log line produced while handling it and propagated to downstream services, so in Kibana you can filter by that one ID and see the complete journey of a single request across every service it touched.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has fifty branches, each keeping its own paper logbook. When a customer complains "my transfer failed," staff would have to phone every branch and flip through separate books. ELK is like scanning every branch's logbook into one central searchable computer. The correlation ID is like stamping a single reference number on every form a customer's request touches as it moves from the teller to the back office to the vault — so later you type that one number into Kibana and instantly see every step the request took, in order, no matter which department handled it.

**One line to remember:** ELK pools every service's logs into one searchable place, and a correlation ID lets you pull the complete story of a single request out of billions of log lines with one filter.

sections.s2_technical:
In a microservices system, logs are a problem precisely because they are scattered. Each service runs in multiple Pods, each Pod writes logs to its own ephemeral filesystem, and a single customer action may touch five services. Without centralization, diagnosing an issue means logging into many Pods and correlating by hand, and when a Pod is recreated its logs vanish. The ELK stack solves this by shipping all logs into one durable, searchable store.

Elasticsearch is the heart. It is a distributed search engine that stores each log line as a JSON document in an index, building an inverted index so that searching across billions of log lines is fast. Logs are usually written into time-based indices, for example one per day, which makes it easy to retain recent data on fast storage and expire or archive old data.

Logstash or Beats does the collection. In a modern Kubernetes setup, a lightweight shipper such as Filebeat runs as a DaemonSet, meaning one agent per node, tailing the container log files, enriching each line with metadata like the Pod name and namespace, and forwarding to Elasticsearch, sometimes via Logstash for heavier parsing. The key enabler is that the application itself logs in structured JSON rather than plain text, so fields like the service name, log level, timestamp, and correlation ID arrive as queryable fields, not as a blob of text you have to parse later.

Kibana is the window. It connects to Elasticsearch and lets engineers run searches in a query language, build visualisations such as error-rate-over-time charts, and assemble dashboards. In practice you configure Kibana by pointing it at the Elasticsearch cluster, creating an index pattern that tells Kibana which indices to read and which field is the timestamp, and then saving searches and dashboards the team reuses. For an on-call engineer, the typical workflow is to open Kibana's Discover view, filter by the service and a time range, and narrow down to the error.

Correlation IDs are what turn centralized logging into true request tracing. When a request first enters the system, usually at the API gateway or the first service, it is assigned a unique correlation ID, often a UUID, or it reuses one supplied in a request header if the call came from another internal service. That ID is placed into the logging context so every log line written during that request automatically includes it. In a Java application this is done with the Mapped Diagnostic Context, or MDC, which is a per-thread map that the logging framework merges into each log line. Crucially, the service also forwards the correlation ID in the headers of any outbound call to a downstream service, and that service reads the header and puts it into its own MDC, so the same ID flows end to end.

The payoff is dramatic. When Rajesh reports a failed transfer, the engineer finds the correlation ID from the error response or an audit record, types it into Kibana, and sees every log line from the gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, and the account service for that one request, in time order, across all Pods. What would have been an hour of cross-referencing becomes a ten-second filter.

The senior-level nuance is the relationship between logging and distributed tracing. Correlation IDs in logs give you the thread to pull, but full distributed tracing tools add timing and a parent-child span relationship so you can also see how long each hop took and where the latency was. A mature setup uses a standard like the W3C traceparent header so the trace ID and the log correlation ID are the same value, letting you jump from a slow trace in a tracing tool straight to the matching logs in Kibana. Two other production concerns matter: never log sensitive data such as full account numbers or passwords into Elasticsearch, because those logs are broadly searchable, and manage index lifecycle so you retain what compliance requires and expire the rest to control cost.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a transfer from Rajesh to Priya passes through an API gateway, the Transfer Service, the Fraud Service, and the Account Service. Rajesh reports that one transfer failed, and the on-call engineer must find out why.

Problem 1 — The four services each run several Pods, and the logs for Rajesh's request are spread across many Pods on many nodes. Without centralization, the engineer cannot even find all the relevant log lines. This is exactly what the ELK stack solves: every service ships structured JSON logs into one Elasticsearch cluster that Kibana can search.

Problem 2 — Even with all logs in one place, there are millions of lines. The engineer needs to isolate just the lines belonging to Rajesh's one failed transfer. This is exactly what a correlation ID solves: the gateway stamped the request with a unique ID that every service attached to every log line, so one filter in Kibana isolates the whole request.

Problem 3 — The correlation ID must travel across service boundaries, not just within one service. If the Transfer Service calls the Fraud Service without passing the ID, the fraud logs would be orphaned. This is exactly what header propagation plus the Mapped Diagnostic Context solve: the ID rides in an HTTP header and is placed into each service's logging context.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that simulates the request flowing through the services, each producing structured log lines tagged with a shared correlation ID, and an in-memory `LogStore` that stands in for Elasticsearch. A `CorrelationContext` models the MDC. A `KibanaQuery` class then filters the store by correlation ID, reproducing exactly what an engineer does in Kibana's Discover view. The demo runs one successful transfer and one failed transfer, then queries by the failed transfer's correlation ID to show the complete cross-service story.


The log shipping configuration is part of the deliverable:

```yaml
# logging/filebeat.yml — one agent per node (DaemonSet), ships to Elasticsearch
filebeat.inputs:
  - type: container
    paths: [ "/var/log/containers/*.log" ]      # tail every container's logs
processors:
  - add_kubernetes_metadata: {}                  # enrich with pod/namespace
output.elasticsearch:
  hosts: [ "https://elasticsearch:9200" ]
  index: "bank-logs-%{+yyyy.MM.dd}"              # time-based daily index
```

```xml
<!-- logging/logback-spring.xml — emit JSON with the MDC correlationId field -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
      <!-- includeMdc puts correlationId into every JSON log line -->
      <includeMdcKeyName>correlationId</includeMdcKeyName>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="JSON"/></root>
</configuration>
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/elk-tracing-1.0.0.jar

# Real Kibana query (Discover view) for a correlation id:
#   correlationId : "cid-1a2b3c4d"
# Or via the Elasticsearch API:
curl -X GET "https://elasticsearch:9200/bank-logs-*/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":{"match":{"correlationId":"cid-1a2b3c4d"}}}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transfer requests from Rajesh to Priya, one for fifty thousand rupees that succeeds and one for nine hundred thousand rupees that the fraud service blocks.

Step 1: The first request arrives at the gateway. The gateway mints a correlation ID, places it into the correlation context, and writes a log line tagged with that ID into the store, which represents indexing a document into Elasticsearch.

Step 2: The gateway calls the Transfer Service, explicitly passing the same correlation ID, mirroring how a real service forwards it in an HTTP header. The Transfer Service writes its own log line with the identical ID, so its logs join the same request story.

Step 3: The Transfer Service calls the Fraud Service with the same ID. The amount of fifty thousand is below the threshold, so the Fraud Service logs a normal score and returns not flagged. The Transfer Service then calls the Account Service, again with the same ID, which logs the debit and credit. Finally the Transfer Service logs that the transfer completed. All of these lines carry one correlation ID.

Step 4: The second request repeats the flow with a fresh correlation ID, but the amount of nine hundred thousand exceeds the fraud threshold. The Fraud Service logs a warning and returns flagged, and the Transfer Service logs an error that the transfer was blocked. This second request's lines all carry a different correlation ID from the first.

Step 5: The demo finds the correlation ID of the blocked request by locating the line containing the blocked message. This mirrors how an engineer would get the ID from an error response or audit record.

Step 6: KibanaQuery filters the entire store by that one correlation ID, exactly as an engineer types the filter into Kibana's Discover view. It returns only the lines for the failed request — the gateway receiving it, the transfer service validating, the fraud service flagging, and the transfer service blocking — in order, across all services. The successful request's lines are excluded because they carry a different ID.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 2:15:40 AM com.bank.elk.kibana.KibanaQuery searchByCorrelationId
INFO: Kibana filter: correlationId = cid-7f3a9b2c
INFO: {"ts":"...","service":"gateway","level":"INFO","correlationId":"cid-7f3a9b2c","msg":"received transfer SAV2001->CUR3001 amount 900000"}
INFO: {"ts":"...","service":"transfer-service","level":"INFO","correlationId":"cid-7f3a9b2c","msg":"validating transfer from SAV2001"}
INFO: {"ts":"...","service":"fraud-service","level":"WARN","correlationId":"cid-7f3a9b2c","msg":"fraud score for SAV2001 flagged=true"}
INFO: {"ts":"...","service":"transfer-service","level":"ERROR","correlationId":"cid-7f3a9b2c","msg":"transfer BLOCKED by fraud rules"}
INFO: 4 log lines across all services for this request
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The ELK stack is three tools that together solve the scattered-logs problem in a microservices system. Elasticsearch is a distributed search engine that stores each log line as a JSON document and builds an inverted index so searching billions of lines is fast. Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect logs from every service and ship them in; in a Kubernetes setup I run Filebeat as a DaemonSet, one agent per node, tailing container logs and enriching them with Pod metadata. And Kibana is the web interface where engineers search, visualise, and build dashboards. I configure Kibana by pointing it at the Elasticsearch cluster, creating an index pattern over the daily log indices with the timestamp field, and saving the searches and dashboards the team reuses.

The thing that makes centralized logging genuinely powerful is the correlation ID. When a request first enters the system at the gateway, I assign it a unique ID, or reuse one passed in a header from an upstream internal service, and I put it into the logging context — in Java that is the Mapped Diagnostic Context, a per-thread map the logging framework merges into every log line. So every line written while handling that request automatically carries the ID. Critically, the service also forwards the ID in the headers of any downstream call, and the next service reads it into its own context, so the same ID flows end to end across every service the request touches.

The payoff is what sells it in an interview. When Rajesh reports a failed transfer, I get the correlation ID from the error response or an audit record, type it into Kibana's Discover view as a single filter, and instantly see every log line from the gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, and the account service for that one request, in time order, across all Pods. What used to be an hour of logging into individual Pods and cross-referencing by hand becomes a ten-second filter that reveals, for example, that the fraud service blocked the transfer because the amount exceeded a threshold.

At National Bank of India I also kept two production disciplines front of mind. First, the correlation ID is tied to our distributed tracing so the trace ID and the log ID are the same value, letting me jump from a slow trace straight to the matching logs. Second, we never logged sensitive data like full account numbers or passwords into Elasticsearch, because those logs are broadly searchable, and we used index lifecycle management to retain what compliance required and expire the rest to control storage cost. So ELK plus correlation IDs did not just make debugging fast; it did so in a way that respected the security and cost realities of a regulated bank.
